growth_story.headline: Pakistan's income per person has grown a steady 1.6 percent a year since 1990, but in short booms broken by repeated crises.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990 Pakistan's income per person has grown at a steady but modest pace, averaging 1.6 percent a year over 1990-2025, with no lasting shift up or down. Inside that single era, growth has come in short spurts and sharp stops: fast years such as 5.2 percent in 2004 and in 2016 gave way to falls in 2008, 2010, 2020 and 2023. The IMF ties the 2008 crisis to security problems and oil and food price shocks, the strains of 2019 to large deficits, loose money and the defense of an overvalued currency, and the 2023 fall to floods, a hard world economy and policy missteps. The World Bank links the pattern to growth that leans on debt and on spending funded by money sent home from abroad, while exports have shrunk as a share of the economy. The last decade averaged 2.0 percent a year, up from 1.4 in the decade before, and income per person reached its highest level yet in 2025.

threads.title: Boom-bust cycles
threads.text: Growth tends to speed up on borrowing and spending, then stop when the money runs short: income per person grew 4.4 percent in 2018, then 0.8 in 2019, and fell 3.0 percent in 2020. The World Bank ties these cycles to growth that depends on debt and on spending of money sent home from abroad. The IMF said the run-up to 2019 brought large deficits, loose money and an overvalued currency.

threads.title: Crises of 2008 and 2023
threads.text: After strong years in the mid-2000s, income per person fell 0.6 percent in 2008 as security problems and oil and food price shocks hit. It fell again by 1.9 percent in 2023, after the 2022 floods, as inflation reached 30.8 percent and reserves ran low.

threads.title: Investment stays low
threads.text: Investment fell from 17.3 percent of GDP in 1990 to 11.5 in 2024 and was 12.6 in 2025. The IMF calls it very low next to similar economies and points to a hard business climate, weak governance and a large role for the state.

since_last_year.text: The recovery from the 2023 slump went on: income per person grew 2.1 percent in 2025 and reached its highest level yet. The 2025 floods and, in 2026, higher world commodity prices pushed inflation up again, though the IMF reported in May 2026 that stability had held despite the Middle East war.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe a boom-bust economy, yet the data find no lasting break since 1990: one era averaging 1.6 percent a year. Both hold because the booms and busts are short and cancel out. The sources also report growth of total output, which runs ahead of income per person because the population keeps growing; income per person grew only 2.1 percent in 2025.
